record.original_question: Suppose that ∞ X f (z) = an z n n=0 is convergent in D, that |z0 | = 1, and that neither of the series ∞ X ∞ X (Re an )z0n , (Im an )z0n , n=0 n=0 is absolutely convergent. Let S be the set of complex values assumed by the series ∞ X εn an z0n , n=0 where ε = ±1, and is allowed to vary over all possible choices. Is it true that S = C? (A. C. Offord; communicated by J. G. Clunie)

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $f(z)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} a_n z^n$ be a power series with complex coefficients $a_n\in\mathbb{C}$ that converges for every $z$ in the open unit disc $\mathbb{D}=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:|z|<1\}$. Fix a point $z_0\in\mathbb{C}$ with $|z_0|=1$, and assume that neither of the two real series
$$\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(\operatorname{Re} a_n)\,z_0^{\,n}, \qquad \sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(\operatorname{Im} a_n)\,z_0^{\,n}$$
is absolutely convergent. For every choice of signs $\varepsilon=(\varepsilon_n)_{n\ge 0}$ with $\varepsilon_n\in\{-1,+1\}$ for each $n$, consider the series
$$\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\varepsilon_n a_n z_0^{\,n},$$
and let $S\subseteq\mathbb{C}\cup\{\text{divergent}\}$ be the set of all complex numbers obtained as the sum of such a series for some sign sequence $\varepsilon$ for which the series converges. Is it true that $S=\mathbb{C}$, i.e., that every complex number is attained as the sum of $\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\varepsilon_n a_n z_0^{\,n}$ for some choice of signs $\varepsilon_n\in\{\pm 1\}$?
artifact.category_tag: Power series on the unit circle
artifact.status_search_result: A targeted web search did not return any results that address this specific question of A. C. Offord on whether the set of sums of sign-flipped power series on the unit circle exhausts the complex plane. No published resolution (positive or negative) was located, and the problem is listed in a long-standing collection of unsolved function-theory problems, but its current status could not be verified from the available sources.
